LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD is a standard binary package for the "ee" editor that downloads a prebuilt release tarball from GitHub. The top-level scope consists only of variable assignments and a simple `case` statement to set `_CARCH` — no `eval`, base64 decoding, or network commands are executed during sourcing. There is no `pkgver()` function that could fetch and run remote code; `pkgver` is a static value (`0.11.5`). The `source_x86_64` entry points to the project's own GitHub releases, and a valid SHA256 checksum is provided. The `build()` and `package()` functions exist but will not execute under `--nobuild --noprepare`. Running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `--printsrcinfo` only fetches and extracts the declared source, which is the intended and safe behavior of those commands.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Standard binary PKGBUILD from GitHub releases; no malicious code in sourced scope.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD is a standard AUR package for the `ee` text editor binary release. The source is downloaded from the project's own official GitHub releases (`https://github.com/ffimnsr/ee/releases/download/v0.11.5/...`), and the SHA256 checksum is properly set (not SKIP), which is good supply-chain hygiene for a prebuilt binary.

The `build()` function simply invokes the downloaded binary to generate shell completions (bash, zsh, fish) — standard application functionality. The `package()` function performs routine installations: copying the binary to `/usr/bin/`, shared data to `/usr/share/`, completions to their respective shell directories, and documentation/license files to standard locations.

There are no suspicious network requests, no obfuscated code, no encoded payloads, no `curl|bash` patterns, no `eval`, no exfiltration attempts, and no unexpected file system modifications. The `options=(!strip)` is common for prebuilt binaries. The minor issue of `${arch[1]}` referencing a non-existent array element is harmless since the case statement only matches the defined architectures.
</details>
<evidence>

<summary>Standard AUR binary packaging of ee editor with proper SHA256 verification.</summary>
</security_assessment>
